unit.title: Perform basic welding using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which part of arc welding harms the eyes and skin, even when you cannot feel it happening?
options: The smell of the burning flux coating
The loud crackle and hiss of the arc
The heat given off by the welding cables
Ultraviolet rays from the arc

questions.stem: What should you do before striking an arc when other people are working nearby?
options: Ask them to watch the arc so they get used to it
Put up screens and warn them to look away
Turn the current down so the arc is less bright
Weld with your helmet up so you can see them

questions.stem: How does a welder most often get an electric shock from MMAW equipment?
options: Wet gloves, wet clothes or standing in water
Touching the plastic case of the machine with dry hands
Standing on a dry wooden board while welding
Holding the electrode holder by its insulated handle

questions.stem: As the welding current goes up, what filter shade is needed in the helmet?
options: A lighter shade (a lower number)
The same shade at every current
A darker shade (a higher number)
No filter, only clear glass

questions.stem: Why should welding fumes be kept out of your breathing zone?
options: They make the arc harder to see through the filter
They hold metal dust and gases that harm the lungs
They make the flux coating fall off the electrode
They make the slag harder to chip off the bead

questions.stem: Why are cotton or wool work clothes safer than nylon or polyester for welding?
options: Nylon lets the arc light pass straight through
Nylon carries electricity much better than cotton
Nylon is too heavy and slows the welder down
Nylon melts and sticks to the skin when it burns

questions.stem: A person has had a shock and is still touching a live welding lead. What should you do first?
options: Grab them by the arm and pull them away at once
Throw water over them to break the contact
Switch off the power first, then help them
Wait for them to let go before doing anything

questions.stem: Before welding, what must be done with oily rags, paper and wood shavings near the bench?
options: Remove them from the area
Cover them with a cotton sheet
Push them under the bench
Wet them a little with oil

questions.stem: What is the main job of the welding machine (power source)?
options: To make the gas that shields the arc
To give a high current at a low voltage
To raise the mains voltage to a higher level
To store electricity in it, like a car battery does

questions.stem: What does the duty cycle on a welding machine's rating plate tell you?
options: How many electrodes it can burn up in one hour
How many times a year it must be serviced by a technician
How much power it takes from the mains each day
How many minutes in 10 it can weld at a set current

questions.stem: A machine is rated 150 A at 60% duty cycle. At 150 A, how long can it weld in every 10 minutes?
options: 10 minutes
4 minutes
6 minutes
1 minute

questions.stem: What is open-circuit voltage (OCV)?
options: The output voltage when on but not welding
The voltage across the arc while you are welding
The voltage of the mains socket on the wall
The voltage left in the cable after switch-off

questions.stem: Where should the work return clamp be fixed?
options: To the leg of the welding bench, far from the joint
To clean metal on the job, close to the weld
To any water pipe that runs near the workshop
To the outside case of the welding machine

questions.stem: Which check should you make on an electrode holder before use?
options: That it has been painted a bright safety colour
That it is heavier than the work clamp
That it is still warm from the last user
That the jaws and insulation are not damaged

questions.stem: With direct current (DC), what decides which polarity to use?
options: The colour of the welding cables
The time of day the job is done
The electrode maker's instructions
The size of the work clamp

questions.stem: How should welding cables be laid out during work?
options: Kept off walkways, untangled and away from hot metal
Coiled tightly on the floor next to the machine
Run through puddles to keep them cool
Hung across the hot work so they are always in reach

questions.stem: What is the metal rod in the middle of an MMAW electrode called?
options: The flux
The stub
The core wire
The slag

questions.stem: What does the flux coating give off as it burns in the arc?
options: Extra current that makes the arc hotter
A thin layer like paint that stops the weld rusting
Water vapour that cools the weld pool
Gas and slag that shield the weld from the air

questions.stem: In the electrode code E7018, what does '70' tell you?
options: The length of the electrode in centimetres
The minimum weld metal strength (70 000 psi)
The current to set, which is 70 amps
The diameter in tenths of a millimetre

questions.stem: Which electrode is a good general-purpose choice for a beginner welding mild steel on AC or DC?
options: E6013 (rutile)
A stainless steel electrode
A cast iron electrode
A hard-facing electrode

questions.stem: Which current range is about right for a 3.2 mm E6013 electrode? (Always check the maker's packet.)
Why must electrodes be kept dry?
options: Wet electrodes weigh more and tire out the welder
Wet electrodes make the arc too quiet to hear well
Damp flux causes porosity, cracking and a poor arc
Wet electrodes rust and turn the weld red

questions.stem: You change from a 3.2 mm electrode to a 2.5 mm electrode. What should you do to the current?
options: Turn it up
Turn it down
Leave it the same
Set it to the top

questions.stem: Why is plate cleaned to bright metal before welding?
options: Rust, paint and oil spoil the weld
Bright metal makes the arc light less harmful
Clean plate needs a bigger electrode
Rust makes the plate too heavy to move

questions.stem: Which are the two usual ways to strike an arc?
options: Dipping and rolling
Pressing and holding
Scratching and tapping
Twisting and pulling

questions.stem: Where should you strike the arc?
options: On the bench top or the vice, away from the job
In the joint, where the weld will cover it
On the face of the plate well away from the joint
On the work clamp to test the current

questions.stem: A good arc length is about the same as which measurement?
options: The full length of the electrode holder jaws
Twice the width of the weld bead
The thickness of the plate
The diameter of the electrode's core wire

questions.stem: When running a bead in the flat position, how is the electrode usually held?
options: At 70–80° to the plate, tilted the way you travel
At exactly 90° to the plate, standing straight up with no tilt
At about 30° to the plate, so it is nearly lying flat
At about 45° to the plate, tilted back the other way

questions.stem: What does too high a current usually cause?
options: A narrow, tall bead that sits on top of the plate
An arc that keeps going out
Spatter, undercut and a red-hot electrode
The electrode sticking to the plate

questions.stem: What does too low a current usually cause?
options: Deep penetration and burn-through
A wide, flat bead with deep undercut
A red-hot electrode that glows along its length
Sticking and a high, narrow bead

questions.stem: What does travelling too slowly usually produce?
options: A thin, narrow bead with long, pointed ripples
A wide, heavy bead that may roll over the edges
An arc that keeps going out every few seconds
A bead with no slag cover left anywhere on it

questions.stem: What should you do at the end of a bead to avoid leaving a crater?
options: Pause briefly to fill the crater, then lift away
Snap the electrode away quickly
Turn the current up high for the last few millimetres
Drag the electrode off the edge of the plate

questions.stem: Why might a welder move the electrode from side to side (weave) as the bead is made?
options: To use up each electrode more slowly and save money
To lower the heat put into the plate
To make the slag easier to chip off
To make a wider bead to fill a wider joint

questions.stem: Which joint is made when two plates lie on top of each other with an overlap?
options: A butt joint
A corner joint
A lap joint
An edge joint

questions.stem: What kind of weld is made in the corner of a tee joint?
options: A butt weld
A fillet weld
A plug weld
A spot weld

questions.stem: Why are parts tack welded before the full weld is made?
options: To hold them in place and in line while welding
To test that the machine is switched on and working
To heat the plate up before the main weld
To mark where the slag will be chipped

questions.stem: Why does a plate bend out of shape (distort) after a long bead?
options: The electrode used was much too long for the job
The work clamp was fixed too loosely
The weld shrinks as it cools and pulls on it
The slag was left on overnight

questions.stem: Which tools are used to remove slag from a bead?
options: A flat file and a sharp scriber
A centre punch and a hammer
A cold chisel and a heavy sledge hammer
A chipping hammer and a wire brush

questions.stem: Why should you wear clear safety glasses when chipping slag?
options: Hot slag chips can fly into the eyes
They make the weld ripples much easier to see
They stop the arc light reaching you
They keep fumes away from your face

questions.stem: What is porosity?
options: A groove melted into the plate beside the bead
Small gas holes trapped in the weld metal
Slag trapped between two weld passes
A crack along the middle of the bead

questions.stem: What are the small balls of metal stuck to the plate around a weld called?
options: Porosity
Undercut
Overlap
Spatter

questions.stem: What is overlap in a weld?
options: A crack across the end of the weld
Small holes made by gas trapped in the weld metal
Weld metal lying on the plate, not fused to it
A groove left in the plate along the toe

questions.stem: What should a good straight bead on flat plate look like?
options: Even width and height, with even ripples
Wide in some places and narrow in others
Covered with small holes along the top
Tall and narrow, standing high on the plate

questions.stem: What should be done at the end of a welding session?
options: Leave the machine on for the next class
Throw hot electrode stubs into the paper bin
Leave the cables lying across the walkway
Switch off, coil the leads, stubs in a metal tin

questions.stem: Jermaine notices that the welding machine's mains cable is cut. What should he do?
options: Wrap the cut with insulating tape and carry on
Unplug it later, after his weld is finished
Stop, tag the machine out of use and report it
Swap the plug to another socket and carry on

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

In the electrode code E6013, what does the letter E stand for?

What do we call how deep the weld melts into the parent metal?

essays.stem: Explain the main hazards of MMAW (electric shock, arc radiation, fumes, fire and burns) and how a welder controls each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Electric shock: the electrode and holder are live whenever the machine is on. Keep gloves and clothing dry, never stand in water, check cables and the holder for damage, and switch off before working on the machine. Arc radiation: the arc gives off ultraviolet and infrared light that burns the eyes and skin. Wear a helmet with the right filter shade, cover all skin, and put up screens to protect other people. Fumes: the flux and the metal give off fumes that harm the lungs. Weld with good ventilation or extraction and keep your head out of the fumes. Fire: sparks and spatter can fly several metres. Clear away anything that burns, keep an extinguisher ready and check the area after work. Burns: metal stays hot long after welding, so use tongs and mark hot work.
markingPoints: Electric shock: dry gloves and clothing, no water, cables and holder checked
Arc radiation: helmet with the right shade, skin covered, screens for others
Fumes: ventilation or extraction, head kept out of the fumes
Fire: burnables cleared, extinguisher ready, area checked after work
Burns: tongs used and hot work marked

essays.stem: Describe the parts of an MMAW welding circuit, and say what each part does.
essays.modelAnswer: The welding machine (power source) takes power from the mains and gives a high current at a low voltage, either AC or DC; the current is set on its controls. The mains plug and cable bring the power in and must be undamaged. The electrode lead carries the current from the machine to the electrode holder. The electrode holder grips the electrode and has an insulated handle so that the welder can hold it safely. The electrode carries the current to the arc and melts to form the weld, while its flux coating shields the weld. The arc jumps from the electrode to the work and melts the metal. The work return lead and clamp carry the current from the work back to the machine, which completes the circuit. All connections must be clean and tight.
markingPoints: Power source gives a high current at a low voltage (AC or DC), set on its controls
Electrode lead and insulated holder carry the current to the electrode
Electrode makes the arc and adds metal; the flux shields the weld
Work return lead and clamp carry the current back to complete the circuit
Connections must be clean and tight for the circuit to work well

essays.stem: Describe the checks and set-up you would carry out before running beads on a mild steel plate.
essays.modelAnswer: First check the work area: screens in place, nothing that can burn, an extinguisher nearby, good ventilation and a dry floor. Put on full PPE: a helmet with the right shade, safety glasses, leather gloves, a jacket and boots. Check the machine: the mains cable and plug are undamaged, the leads are not cut or burnt, the connections are tight and the electrode holder's jaws and insulation are in good order. Clean the plate to bright metal with a wire brush or grinder and lay it flat on the bench. Fix the work clamp to clean metal near the weld. Choose the electrode, for example 3.2 mm E6013, and check that it is dry and undamaged. Set the polarity and current from the packet and test on scrap plate. Warn people nearby before striking the arc.
markingPoints: Work area made safe: screens, burnables cleared, extinguisher, ventilation, dry floor
Full PPE put on
Machine, leads, holder and connections checked
Plate cleaned and work clamp fixed near the weld
Electrode chosen and checked, current set from the packet and tested on scrap

essays.stem: Explain how you choose the electrode type, size and current for a job, and how you would test the current setting.
essays.modelAnswer: First find the parent metal, its thickness and the welding position from the drawing or job sheet. Choose an electrode type to suit the metal: for example E6013 for general mild steel work, or a low-hydrogen E7018 where a stronger, crack-resistant weld is needed. Choose the size to suit the thickness: a 2.5 mm electrode for thin plate, 3.2 mm for medium plate, and larger for thicker plate. Then read the current range and polarity on the electrode packet, and set the machine near the middle of the range. Run a short bead on scrap plate of the same thickness. If the electrode sticks and the bead is high and narrow, turn the current up a little; if there is a lot of spatter and undercut, turn it down. Adjust until the arc is steady and the bead is even.
markingPoints: Finds the metal, thickness and position from the drawing or job sheet
Chooses the electrode type to suit the metal and the job
Chooses the electrode size to suit the thickness
Sets current and polarity from the maker's packet
Tests on scrap of the same thickness and adjusts from what the bead shows

essays.stem: Describe how to strike an arc and run a straight bead on flat plate. Include the arc length, the electrode angle and the travel speed.
essays.modelAnswer: Put on PPE and check the current. Hold the electrode just above the start of the line, lower the helmet, then strike the arc by scratching the tip on the plate like a match, or by tapping it lightly, and lift it at once to the right length. Keep the arc length about the same as the core wire diameter, about 3 mm for a 3.2 mm electrode, and keep it steady by feeding the electrode down as it burns away. Hold the electrode at about 70–80° to the plate, tilted in the direction of travel. Move along the line at a steady speed so that the bead has an even width and even ripples. At the end, pause to fill the crater, then lift away. Chip off the slag, brush the bead and check it.
markingPoints: Strikes by scratching or tapping, then lifts to the right length
Arc length about the core wire diameter, kept steady by feeding down
Electrode at about 70–80° to the plate, tilted in the direction of travel
Steady travel speed giving an even width and ripples
Fills the crater at the end, then cleans and checks the bead

essays.stem: Explain the effects of wrong current and wrong travel speed on a bead, and how you can tell these faults apart.
essays.modelAnswer: If the current is too low, the electrode sticks, the arc is hard to keep going, and the bead is high and narrow with poor fusion at the edges. If the current is too high, there is a lot of spatter, the electrode glows red, the bead is wide and flat, and there may be undercut or even burn-through. If travel is too fast, the bead is thin and narrow, with long, pointed ripples, and may not fuse well. If travel is too slow, the bead is wide and heavy, may roll over the edges, and slag can run ahead of the pool. To tell them apart, watch the arc and the electrode as well as the bead: current faults change how the arc behaves and how hot the electrode gets, while speed faults mainly change the width of the bead and the shape of the ripples.
markingPoints: Current too low: sticking, unsteady arc, high narrow bead, poor fusion
Current too high: spatter, red-hot electrode, wide flat bead, undercut
Travel too fast: thin narrow bead with pointed ripples
Travel too slow: wide heavy bead, overlap, slag running ahead
Explains how to tell current faults from speed faults

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and weld a lap joint in 6 mm mild steel plate laid flat on the bench.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean the edges and faces of both plates to bright metal. Lay one plate on top of the other with an overlap of about 25 mm and clamp them flat to the bench. Tack weld at each end and check that the plates are tight together. Choose a 3.2 mm E6013 electrode and set the current from the packet, then test it on scrap. Point the electrode into the corner between the edge of the top plate and the face of the bottom plate, at about 45°, and tilt it about 10–20° in the direction of travel. Keep a short arc and a steady speed so that both the plate edge and the face below are melted in. Fill the crater at the end. Chip off the slag and check that the fillet has equal legs, is fused to both plates and has no undercut on the top edge.
markingPoints: Cleans the plates and clamps them with a suitable overlap
Tacks at each end and checks the plates are tight together
Chooses the electrode and sets and tests the current
Correct electrode angles, short arc and steady speed into the corner
Cleans and checks the fillet: equal legs, fused to both plates, no undercut

essays.stem: Name four common faults in MMAW beads. For each, give one cause and one way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Porosity is small gas holes in the weld. It is caused by damp electrodes, dirty plate or too long an arc. Prevent it by keeping electrodes dry, cleaning the plate and holding a short arc. Undercut is a groove melted along the toe of the weld. It is caused by too high a current, too long an arc or the wrong angle. Prevent it with the right current, a short arc and the correct angle. Slag inclusions are slag trapped in the weld. They are caused by poor cleaning between runs or too low a current. Prevent them by chipping and brushing every run and using the right current. Lack of fusion is weld metal that has not melted into the plate. It is caused by low current or travelling too fast. Prevent it with the right current and a steady speed.
markingPoints: Porosity, with a correct cause and prevention
Undercut, with a correct cause and prevention
Slag inclusions, with a correct cause and prevention
Lack of fusion (or spatter or overlap), with a correct cause and prevention
Uses correct trade terms throughout

essays.stem: Explain why steel plates move and bend (distort) when they are welded, and how tack welds and other methods help to control this.
essays.modelAnswer: When a weld is made, the weld metal and the plate next to it get very hot and expand. As they cool, the weld metal shrinks and pulls on the plate, so the plate bends or twists towards the weld. This is distortion. Tack welds hold the parts in place and in line, so they cannot move far while the full weld is made; tacks go at each end and evenly along long joints. Clamping the parts to the bench or a jig also holds them. Pre-setting the parts at a small angle lets the weld pull them straight as it shrinks. Using the right current and not putting in more weld than needed reduces the heat. On long joints, welding in short runs or from the middle outwards spreads the heat more evenly.
markingPoints: Heat makes the metal expand, and the weld shrinks and pulls as it cools
Tack welds hold the parts in place and in line
Clamps or a jig hold the parts during welding
Pre-setting lets the weld pull the parts straight
Less heat and short or balanced runs reduce distortion

essays.stem: Describe how to finish a welding session safely: shutting down, cleaning up, storing electrodes and reporting faults.
essays.modelAnswer: Finish the last weld and fill the crater. Take the stub out of the holder and hang the holder up where it cannot touch the work or the bench. Switch off the machine at its own switch and at the mains. Coil the leads loosely and hang them up off the floor. Put electrode stubs in a metal container, not a paper bin, as they may still be hot. Put unused electrodes back in their packet or in the electrode oven so that they stay dry. Leave hot test pieces to cool, or handle them with tongs, and mark them hot. Sweep up slag and spatter and check the area for anything smouldering. Report any damaged cable, holder or clamp, or any fault with the machine, to the instructor, and tag it out of use.
markingPoints: Removes the stub and hangs up the holder safely
Switches off at the machine and the mains, and coils the leads
Stubs in a metal container; unused electrodes stored dry
Hot work marked or handled with tongs; area swept and checked for fire
Faults reported to the instructor and faulty items tagged out of use

practical1.title: Running straight and weave beads on mild steel plate
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a safe MMAW welding bay and run beads on 10 mm mild steel plate (about 150 mm × 150 mm, one plate for each member) in the flat position, using 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes. Each member sets the current from the packet, tests it on scrap, then runs at least five straight (stringer) beads side by side and two weave beads while the assessor watches. Every member chips and brushes their own beads and checks another member's plate for faults. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 10 mm mild steel plate, about 150 mm × 150 mm (one per member), plus scrap plate for testing
MMAW machine with leads, electrode holder and work clamp
Chipping hammer, wire brush, and soapstone or chalk for marking lines
Tongs and a metal bin for stubs
photos: The welding bay set up with screens in place, and every member in full PPE
A plate cleaned and marked with lines for the beads
The test bead on scrap plate after setting the current
A plate with five straight beads, cleaned of slag
Two weave beads, cleaned of slag
The bay cleaned, the machine off and stubs in a metal bin
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout (helmet with a suitable shade, safety glasses, gloves, jacket, boots)
Checked the machine, leads, holder and clamp, and fixed the clamp near the work
Set the current from the electrode packet and tested it on scrap
Struck the arc in the right place and held a short, steady arc
Straight beads are of even width and height, in straight lines, with even ripples
Weave beads are of even width with no undercut at the edges
Removed all slag and pointed out faults on another member's plate
Left the bay safe: machine off, leads coiled, stubs in a metal bin
safety: Weld only in a screened bay; warn others before striking an arc
Keep gloves and clothing dry, and never stand in water
Remove anything that can burn; keep an extinguisher at hand
Wear clear safety glasses under the helmet when chipping slag
Treat all plate as hot: use tongs and mark hot work

practical2.title: Fillet welds on a lap joint and a tee joint in mild steel plate
practical2.brief: As a group, weld lap joints and tee joints in 6 mm mild steel plate (pieces about 150 mm × 50 mm) with single-run fillet welds, using 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes, with the joints laid on the bench. Share the joints so that both types are made: each member cleans, fits and tacks one joint and welds it while the assessor watches. Each member then cleans their weld and checks it by eye and with a fillet gauge, and the group lays all the joints out for the photos. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 6 mm mild steel plate, about 150 mm × 50 mm (2 pieces per member)
MMAW machine with leads, electrode holder and work clamp
Engineer's square, G-clamps, chipping hammer and wire brush
Angle grinder or power wire brush for cleaning
photos: Plates cleaned, with every member in full PPE
A lap joint tacked and clamped
A tee joint tacked and checked square
A finished lap joint fillet weld, cleaned
A finished tee joint fillet weld, cleaned
The fillet gauge on a finished weld
The bay cleaned, with stubs in a metal bin
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly, including safety glasses when chipping and grinding
Cleaned the plates and tacked the joint tight and in line (tee checked square)
Set the current from the packet and tested it on scrap
Pointed the electrode into the corner at the right angles, with a short arc
Fillet is even, with equal legs, fused to both plates and with no undercut
Removed all slag and checked the weld with a fillet gauge
Left the bay safe and tidy, with stubs in a metal bin
safety: Weld only in a screened bay; warn others before striking an arc
Wear a face shield and safety glasses when grinding; check the disc and the guard
Keep gloves and clothing dry, and never stand in water
Make sure the area is ventilated and keep your head out of the fumes
Treat all metal as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
